holidays.name: New Year's Day (Ganjitsu)
holidays.notes: Most small shops, restaurants, and some attractions close Jan 1-3. Shrines get huge crowds for hatsumōde (first shrine visit). Trains still run.

holidays.name: Coming of Age Day (Seijin no Hi)
holidays.notes: Second Monday of January. Celebrates 20-year-olds; ceremonies bring festive kimono crowds to major shrines.

holidays.name: National Foundation Day
holidays.notes: A quiet public holiday. Most things open as normal.

holidays.name: Emperor's Birthday
holidays.notes: Imperial Palace inner grounds open for public greeting.

holidays.name: Vernal Equinox Day (Shunbun no Hi)
holidays.notes: Falls on or near the first day of spring. Parks busy with early sakura viewing.

holidays.name: Shōwa Day (start of Golden Week)
holidays.notes: Golden Week kicks off. Domestic travel spikes; Shinkansen, flights, and top hotels sell out 2-4 weeks ahead. Prices peak.

holidays.name: Constitution Memorial Day
holidays.notes: Middle of Golden Week. Expect crowds everywhere; museums can be packed.

holidays.name: Children's Day
holidays.notes: Last day of Golden Week. Carp streamers (koinobori) fly across the city.

holidays.name: Marine Day (Umi no Hi)
holidays.notes: Third Monday of July. Beach towns crowd up.

holidays.name: Mountain Day (Yama no Hi)
holidays.notes: Introduced in 2016; Mt. Takao and other trails get busier.

holidays.name: Sports Day (Taiiku no Hi)
holidays.notes: Second Monday of October. Schools and community events flood parks.

holidays.name: Culture Day
holidays.notes: Free admission at many museums and palaces — plan early.

holidays.name: New Year shutdown begins (not official)
holidays.notes: Many small businesses close Dec 29 - Jan 3. Department stores stay open until Dec 30 or 31; konbini never close.

festivals.name: Cherry blossom season (Sakura)
festivals.body: Tokyo's sakura forecast peaks around the last week of March. Top viewing: Ueno Park, Shinjuku Gyoen, Chidorigafuchi (boat rentals), Meguro River (night illumination). Picnic tarps go down at dawn for evening parties.

festivals.name: Sanja Matsuri
festivals.body: Asakusa's biggest festival — 100+ portable shrines (mikoshi) parade around Sensō-ji. Streets are packed shoulder-to-shoulder.

festivals.name: Sumida River Fireworks
festivals.body: Tokyo's oldest and biggest fireworks display — ~20,000 rockets. Asakusa / Skytree area closed to traffic; best viewpoints rooftop bookings sell out months ahead.

festivals.name: Obon
festivals.body: Ancestor-remembering holiday period; domestic travel rivals Golden Week. Many businesses shut for 3-4 days. Bon Odori folk dances light up local plazas.

festivals.name: Autumn colours (Kōyō)
festivals.body: Tokyo's peak foliage lands around late November. Best spots: Rikugien Garden (night illumination), Mt. Takao, Meiji Jingu Gaien, Ichō Namiki ginkgo avenue near Aoyama.

festivals.name: Winter illuminations
festivals.body: Millions of LEDs light up Marunouchi, Omotesando, Roppongi Hills, Tokyo Midtown, and Caretta Shiodome. Free to wander; Starbucks at prime corners fills early.

festivals.name: Comiket (summer)
festivals.body: World's largest fan-comics convention at Tokyo Big Sight. Hotels in Odaiba / Tokyo Bay sell out; taxi queues for cosplayers stretch for blocks.
